1#_: (Siman 87, seif 3.) And the flesh of a wild animal and fowl etc. is permitted in cooking and in benefit etc. This ruling was written by the Rambam, and it must be explained from the passage in chapter Kol HaBasar, daf 113, regarding that the word kid serves as an exclusion for wild animals and impure fowl. And the Talmud questions this according to Shmuel: but we require the word kid to include the carcass! And it answers: Shmuel holds that ein issur chal al issur, etc. If so, according to us, who hold that ein issur chal al issur, we necessarily require the word kid to include both the prohibition of cooking with milk and the carcass, as the Talmud's question implies. And if so, from where do we derive that kid comes to exclude wild animals, fowl, and non-kosher animals? And do not say that the Rambam holds that it is more reasonable to establish the word kid as excluding wild animals and fowl rather than as including the carcass — unlike Shmuel — for if so, what compelled the Talmud there on daf 116, where it holds that Rabbi Akiva maintains issur chal al issur, to say that it is more reasonable to establish the verse as excluding wild animals and fowl rather than as including the carcass? Rather, perforce: were it not that Rabbi Akiva holds issur chal al issur, we would establish the verse as including the carcass. And if so, a difficulty arises, for it states there: it was stated — regarding one who cooks forbidden fat in milk — Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi: one says he is liable to lashes and one says he is not liable. Regarding eating, everyone agrees it is forbidden. The dispute is regarding cooking. The one who says he is liable holds that it is one single prohibition. And the one who says he is not liable holds: since the Torah expressed it in the language of cooking, this comes to teach that since one is not liable to lashes for eating it, one is also not liable to lashes for cooking it. If so, according to the one who says one is liable for cooking because it is one single prohibition, we do not need a verse for cooking to include the carcass. And if the word kid comes to include the carcass in order to forbid eating it — that is not consistent with the semantic implication of the inclusive force of the word kid. And as for what is said — that from the superfluous element in the verse you shall not cook we derive the prohibition regarding eating — nevertheless, certainly the inclusion written in the verse does not apply to eating alone, for eating is not stated explicitly in the verse. Therefore, certainly kid comes to exclude wild animals and fowl. And as for the fact that the Talmud earlier required the explanation that Rabbi Akiva holds issur chal al issur — that is according to the one who says: since one is not liable to lashes for eating it, one is also not liable to lashes for cooking it. In that case, we indeed need the word kid to include the carcass, that is, to render one liable for cooking it. Therefore they were compelled to conclude that he holds issur chal al issur. Thus there is no difficulty with the Rambam, who holds like the one who says one is liable for cooking; therefore kid comes to exclude wild animals and fowl. Investigate this carefully.
2#_: (There, seif 4, in the hagahah) And it appears that according to this, all the more so it is forbidden to cook l'chatchila, etc. See in the Acharonim what they seek to resolve the difficulty of the Darkei Moshe, who left the words of the Rashba requiring further study. And one can say: granted, regarding non-kosher meat with kosher milk, etc. — there is reason to say that since in any case it is forbidden on account of its non-kosher status, it is an uncommon matter that anyone would come to cook it, and regarding an uncommon matter the Rabbis did not issue a decree upon it. Which is not the case with human milk, for by this very reason there is no prohibition whatsoever, and there is reason to be concerned, etc. And note carefully.
3#_: (There, seif 5) "Eggs found in birds, etc., even though it is attached by sinews, etc." See in the Taz what he raised as a difficulty against the opinion of the Rashbam and the Mordechai. And from the words of the Shach, subsection 10, it appears that he interprets the position of the Rashbam — who wrote that it must specifically be developed to the point of having a hard shell — not as his interpretation of the definition of "fully formed eggs," but rather because he holds like Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and is uncertain about the meaning of "attached by sinews." But this is not necessarily so, for one can certainly validly say that the Rashbam interprets the words of the baraita such that "fully formed eggs" means that the shell has been completed. And as for the fact that the Gemara there asks "in accordance with whom? Like Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov" — which implies that Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov is more stringent — one can validly say that he is indeed more stringent, and the interpretation of the baraita is as follows: it states, "if one found fully formed eggs in it, they are permitted to be eaten with kutach" — meaning even l'chatchila, but specifically if the shell has been completed; but if the hard shell has not been completed, it is forbidden to eat them l'chatchila with kutach. But b'dieved, it is implied from the view of the Tanna Kamma that there is no prohibition whatsoever — whether the eggs are fully formed or not fully formed — with regard to b'dieved. If so, according to the Tanna Kamma, the egg does not render garments impure at the gullet. And regarding this, the Beit Yosef states: if they were attached by sinews, they are forbidden even b'dieved. And this validly explains the Gemara's question "in accordance with whom? Like Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov," for according to the Rabbis, we do not distinguish at all between fully formed and not fully formed with regard to b'dieved — and if so, the egg would not render the garments impure at the gullet — therefore it must be like Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov. Or one can say that certainly the Rashbam also held that the Tanna Kamma's position is that once the white and the yolk have been completed, it is also permitted, but since not everyone is expert enough to assess which stage is called "completed," they gave the measure that there must be a hard shell, for then the egg has emerged from doubt. And Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov holds that the entire prohibition regarding the white and the yolk depends only on whether the egg is attached by sinews — and therefore, even if the white and yolk have been completed, if it is still attached by sinews, it is also forbidden. Therefore, it is valid that the Gemara there asks "in accordance with whom? Like Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov," for it teaches: one who eats from the cluster of eggs — meaning if they are still attached by sinews — they are still neveilah. Therefore it must be that the baraita follows Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, for if it were according to the Rabbis, how could the baraita teach without qualification "one who eats from the cluster of eggs, etc." — for according to the Rabbis, sometimes a cluster of eggs is not neveilah — namely, if the white and the yolk have been completed. Therefore it must follow Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, who holds that everything depends on whether the eggs are attached by sinews, and it is valid to state regarding the cluster of eggs that since they are attached by sinews, they have the status of neveilah itself. And study this carefully.
4#_: (Ibid.) "Exempt, and one does not receive lashes for eating them, etc." See in siman 88, where he wishes to prove from the words of Tosafot, chapter 25, daf 114, s.v. HaMevashel b'Mei Chalav, that "exempt" means exempt and it is permitted to cook l'chatchila. For Tosafot wrote: "One who cooks in milk whey is exempt, but there is indeed a prohibition, for kuttach is made from milk whey, and we said above that it is forbidden to eat meat with kuttach" — implying that only in that case is it forbidden l'chatchila, but other things where we do not find explicitly that they are forbidden, it is permitted to cook them l'chatchila. But his words have no basis whatsoever. On the contrary, from there it is proven that "exempt" here means exempt but forbidden. For one could ask: how does Tosafot bring proof from kuttach, which is forbidden to eat, to the matter of cooking — perhaps it is only forbidden to eat, but to cook is permitted even l'chatchila? It must therefore be that Tosafot holds that anything that is forbidden to eat is likewise forbidden to cook l'chatchila. If so, the same applies to all other prohibitions that our Sages forbade to eat on account of basar b'chalav — cooking is likewise forbidden.
5#_:
(Ibid.:) "And one does not receive lashes for eating it on account of basar b'chalav." This implies that, however, on account of blood one would receive lashes, even though it is dam shevishlo (blood that was cooked). It must therefore be said that he holds to distinguish between congealed and liquid blood: if it is congealed, one is not liable for dam shevishlo; and if it is liquid, one is liable. With this, what appeared at first glance as a contradiction in his words is resolved — for above in the laws of salting he wrote and implied many times that dam shevishlo is only d'rabbanan, whereas here it implies the opposite. Rather, it is certainly as stated above. And the source he cites for the Rambam and the Mechaber to distinguish between congealed and liquid is Tosafot in tractate Zevachim.

{Gloss: What the Gaon, the author, wrote — that this is found in Tosafot of Zevachim — it seems that in Zevachim this statement of Tosafot is not found, and perhaps it is a scribal error, and it should read "in Menachot" (daf 21a, s.v. "kan"), for thus it is found there in Tosafot according to Rashi there. However, the matter requires further study, for according to Rashi there is no practical halachic difference at all in this — since according to Rashi even for congealed blood one is liable, and he holds that Rava disagrees there with Ze'iri. Moreover, Ze'iri's own statement that dam shevishlo is exempt applies only to the inner sin-offerings, but for the outer sin-offerings, and all the more so for chulin, even for congealed blood one is liable. According to Rashi's opinion there, that distinction between congealed and liquid applies only to congealing in the sun, but blood cooked in fire certainly always drains out, as is explained there.

But in truth, to settle the Rambam's words more satisfactorily, it appears better to say as the Beit Yosef wrote here: that the Rambam holds like Rashi that dam shevishlo is truly liable with lashes. And as for what the Beit Yosef wondered regarding the sugya in Menachot mentioned above — perhaps he holds that the sugya of Menachot does not follow the halacha — though he did not clarify from where the Rambam derived that it does not follow the halacha. But in truth, according to what Rashi wrote there, it is evident that Rava disagrees with that statement, and Rava is the later authority. A great proof for this is that the Rambam does not cite at all in his laws the ruling of Ze'iri that one does not transgress for dam shevishlo, and therefore he must hold that it was rejected from the halacha.

And as for what the Tur and the Mechaber copied the language of the Rambam — even though they certainly hold that dam shevishlo is d'rabbanan, as the Tur wrote at the end of siman 76 in the name of the Rashba explicitly [and so too the Mechaber, it is explained in many places that he holds it to be d'rabbanan] — and the Drisha already pointed this out here — I say there is no difficulty: since nowadays there are no lashes, they did not bother to be precise in this; and something similar is found in many places, and it is obvious. End of the gloss of the distinguished Gaon, etc., Moreinu HaRav Shlomo HaKohen, may his light shine, Moreh Tzedek of the holy community of Vilna.}
6#_: (There, in the Hagahah:) Some say it is forbidden to stoke a fire under the pot of a non-Jew, etc. Even though it is the meat of a non-Jew and is neveilah, and [therefore the principle of] ein issur chal al issur [might be invoked] — one must say: since even according to the view of the poskim who hold that ta'am k'ikar is d'oraisa in other prohibitions — that applies [only] when a k'zayit became mixed [in a quantity consumed] within k'dei achilat pras; but in [the case of] basar b'chalav, even less than a k'zayit [consumed] within k'dei achilat pras is d'oraisa — according to this, one can say there is no [invocation of] ein issur chal al issur here. Namely, if a k'zayit of neveilah meat fell into ten k'zeitim or more [of milk]: if so, regarding the neveilah [prohibition], the milk does not become forbidden, since there is no k'zayit within k'dei achilat pras; but regarding basar b'chalav, the milk is forbidden. If so, one can say the Rama was concerned for the view of the poskim — thus [ruling] stringently.
7#_:
(ibid.) They further wrote that the vessel in which water is prepared for washing, etc., which is made from the ash upon the stove, etc. The Tzemach Tzedek raised the question: is it not established law that the ash of a stove impairs flavor? If so, what is the concern, since its taste has already been impaired?

One can answer: the Tosafot in the chapter Gid HaNasheh, daf 100b, wrote as follows: According to the interpretation of R' Eliezer, it is well understood why the Torah commanded to kasher all utensils, etc. — for do not the initial waters produced during kashering, etc., carry the absorbed taste and return and render things forbidden, etc. And one might say: when a utensil is not ben yomo, one koshers it, since the Torah only prohibited a pot that is ben yomo. But commentators raise the objection: how would this have helped if one were to kasher those that are not ben yomo? — for then one would have to say that the Torah also prohibited noten taam lifgam; if so, the question still returns to its original place, that the waters give taste and return and render things forbidden.

And one can answer: the Rambam wrote that the reason noten taam lifgam is permitted is because it is used not in the normal manner of deriving benefit from the forbidden substance. But regarding basar b'chalav, the Bach holds that using it not in the normal manner of deriving benefit is also subject to liability, as stated in Pesachim daf 26. If so, a new ruling emerges according to the Rambam's approach: if the taste of meat or milk was absorbed into a pot and it impairs flavor, it is permitted, since it is not considered basar b'chalav at all — for there is no taste of meat here to render the milk forbidden, since the taste of the meat impairs flavor. But this is not so if the pot was already rendered forbidden through cooking basar b'chalav — even if it is not ben yomo and its taste has also been impaired, it is nonetheless forbidden, since it has already been rendered nevelah through basar b'chalav. And even though the taste has now been impaired, even so it is forbidden, for in basar b'chalav even using it not in the normal manner of deriving benefit is also forbidden.

According to this, there is no difficulty with the Rama. For here we are dealing with the prohibition of basar b'chalav: even though it is impaired, it is nevertheless forbidden. And with this, the aforementioned words of the Tosafot are also resolved. For what it says — that when a vessel is not ben yomo one koshers it — is not because of concern for other prohibitions, regarding which it is correctly established that noten taam lifgam is permitted. Rather, what it writes — that the Torah required commanding the kashering of a vessel that is not ben yomo — is because of the concern that perhaps the gentile had been cooking basar b'chalav in it, in which case even noten taam lifgam is also forbidden.

And if so, one cannot raise the objection: but the waters themselves give taste and thus render other things forbidden! This is not a valid objection, for it is established law that regarding a prohibition of mashehu, one does not apply chatichah naaseit nevelah. For if we were to say that in all Torah prohibitions noten taam lifgam is forbidden, then the established law that taam k'ikar d'oraisa applies even to noten taam lifgam would truly be d'oraisa, and one could correctly apply chatichah naaseit nevelah to it. But now that we say that in all Torah prohibitions noten taam lifgam is permitted, therefore the ruling that basar b'chalav is forbidden even when it impairs flavor is only like a prohibition of mashehu, and regarding mashehu one does not apply chatichah naaseit nevelah. Deliberate on this carefully.
8#_:
(Ibid., seif 9) The milk found in the stomach, etc. And some interpret that he rules it forbidden, and it is noted that this is the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam, who rules it forbidden when it is liquid, and the case deals with liquid milk. So too the Mechaber wrote above in siman 81, seif 5 and seif 11, regarding milk found in the stomach of a kosher animal that nursed from a treifa. This was the difficulty Rabbeinu Tam had with the baraita's teaching that a stomach cooked in its own milk is forbidden — for this cannot be reconciled according to the approach of the Rif, who holds that after the return it has the status of mere excretion in all cases, even when the milk within it is liquid. If so, why would a stomach cooked in its milk be forbidden? He was therefore compelled to distinguish between coagulated and liquid: when the stomach is cooked in its milk, this refers to the liquid. And at first glance it appears that Rabbeinu Tam interprets the distinction between before the return and after the return as follows: before the return, he held that the milk does not have the status of mere excretion; after the return, the established ruling is that it does have the status of mere excretion in all cases — and this applies to the coagulated milk. But it is certain that whether before the return or after the return, if the milk does not have the status of excretion, it has the status of the animal's own body and is forbidden. Therefore, liquid milk, which does not have the status of excretion, should be characterized as having the status of the animal's own body. If so, a treifa that nursed from a kosher animal should also be forbidden with respect to liquid milk. This would present a difficulty with what the Mechaber wrote — "and some rule it forbidden regarding the liquid that nursed from the treifa" — which implies that a treifa that nursed from a kosher animal is permitted even regarding the liquid. And according to what was stated above regarding Rabbeinu Tam's approach, there is no basis for this distinction. It must therefore be said according to Rabbeinu Tam that the coagulated milk — whether before or after the return — was always permitted, being counted as mere excretion.

But the distinction between before the return and afterward refers to the liquid: before the return, he held that the liquid has the status of the animal's own body, and therefore a treifa that nursed from a kosher animal is also forbidden, as it is like the animal's own body. But afterward, he held that it does not have the status of the animal's own body. This vindicates the words of the Mechaber above in siman 81, where he wrote that specifically a kosher animal that nursed from a treifa is forbidden — because it does not have the status of mere excretion — whereas a treifa that nursed from a kosher animal: even though it also does not have the status of mere excretion, nevertheless it is not considered the animal's own body but rather as something gathered within it, and it is permitted. This is also evident in Tosafot in tractate Avodah Zarah, daf 35a.

And it is possible to say that what the Mechaber wrote here — "and some rule it forbidden" — reflects the approach of Rashi, who holds that even after the return, even the coagulated milk is not counted as mere excretion. Rather, the distinction between before the return and afterward is: before the return, he held that the milk has the status of the animal's body; after the return, he held that it does not have the status of the animal's body. And as for the Gemara's statement — "the halacha is: one may not curdle using a non-kosher substance, but one may curdle using a kosher substance, etc." — the question remains regarding a kosher stomach that nursed from a treifa: why is this so, since it does not have the status of mere excretion? One can answer that the Sages forbade it only in its intact state, but this halachic ruling pertains to the matter of curdling — regarding the remaining substance, it is permitted. That is to say, in such a case the Sages did not extend their stringency to forbid the cheese. Reflect well on this.

[Gloss: This is puzzling, for Rashi in the Mishnah there implies that if the stomach is forbidden, it is forbidden even to curdle with it. And as for the difficulty raised regarding the halachic ruling — the matter is straightforward, for Rashi does not have the reading "and regarding a kosher stomach that nursed from a treifa," and so too wrote the Maharib there. End of the gloss of Mohar'sh HaKohen, may his light shine, Moreh Tzedek of the community.]
9#_: (There, in the hagahah) And if one curdled cheese in it, etc. — until there is sixty parts of milk against the liquid. And one can say: if the stomach is forbidden only through salting, to the measure of a peel, as the Mechaber and Rama wrote below in siman 98 that one does not need sixty against the peel that became forbidden — it must be said that this is like broth. And although through salting only the measure of a peel is forbidden, broth is more stringent than salting and forbids the entire quantity. And see Shach s.k. 88, seif 40, etc.
10#_:
(Ibid.) And if there was sixty in the milk, everything is permitted. See Shach s.k. 37, who challenged: for us, a curdling agent is not nullified — see his words at length. And one can say: the Tosafot wrote on Avodah Zarah daf 35a, s.v. chada katani, etc., that nevertheless in our locale they curdle cheese in a stomach; R' Yitzchak, son of R' Chaim, said there is some reason to forbid it because the stomach was salted in its skin and there is a basar b'chalav prohibition through salting — for salting is like boiling, etc. — see there. And they challenge: why mention the reason of basar b'chalav, which is only d'rabbanan through salting? It should have mentioned the reason of nevelah taste absorbed in the stomach skin through salting, which would be a d'oraisa prohibition. And they resolve: if the reason were nevelah absorbed in the stomach, we would not forbid because of curdling — for the stomach itself is the curdling agent and is heter; therefore they mention the reason of basar b'chalav, for the stomach itself is also like the body of the prohibition, and they correctly say regarding it that it is a curdling agent and is not nullified. And so too Rama's words here can be explained: since through pickling and salting it is not forbidden d'oraisa through basar b'chalav but only that Chazal forbade it, therefore it is not so stringent that the milk should be considered the body of the prohibition and we do not say regarding it that a curdling agent is not nullified; therefore sixty helps, as Shach wrote s.k. 30 — see there. Investigate.

[Gloss: And even though in those Tosafot, in name of R' Yitzchak, they wished to forbid for this reason — one can say the Tosafot deal when there is not sixty. And one can explain that the Tosafot challenge there: it should have been easy to establish Shmuel's words even before the return, etc. — end of gloss of Rav Shlomo HaKohen, Vilna.]
11#_: (Ibid.) And if the stomach was liquid and coagulated, etc. — and some are lenient in this. It appears from Tosafot that they challenged: why not establish the entire discussion before the return? And that which they do not say "because of the stomach itself" — because the main curdling is in the coagulated part, lest the Gemara holds that perhaps it was liquid at first; or the Tosafot hold like those who are lenient. However, from Tosafot's conclusion it appears the opposite, like those who forbid — as written in the previous s.k. And if they hold like those who forbid, they resolve well: since at first they do not separate the liquid, and afterward the liquid coagulates and is fit to curdle in, it is properly a curdling agent. Investigate.
